profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a mid-sized developer tools company about turning insights from the survey on neural code intelligence into a new internal product direction: an AI assistant for codebase understanding inside the company's IDE extension. The context is that leadership wants one promising prototype concept for the next quarter that goes beyond single-file code completion and focuses on real code intelligence use cases such as onboarding, code navigation, and change comprehension. The agenda is to generate candidate feature directions, narrow them to a plausible prototype shape, and identify what existing infrastructure can be reused. The expected outcome is informal alignment on one prototype concept, a rough idea of what 'repo-level' support should look like, and what would count as a successful pilot by the end of the quarter.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.role: Staff ML Engineer, Applied Code Intelligence
members.expertise: Code LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation, offline evaluation for developer tooling
members.background: Former research engineer who built benchmark pipelines for code search and summarization models before joining the product ML team two years ago.
members.private_state: She wants the brainstorm to land on a prototype narrow enough to implement with current ML infrastructure and to avoid a commitment that would require new serving systems or broad user support this quarter.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'repo-level' in early-stage code intelligence, they usually mean a single checked-out service repository rather than the whole company monorepo.

The 'existing retrieval layer' naturally refers to the mature vector index and chunking pipeline from the internal code search service, because that is the only reusable component she considers production-ready.

For a first mixed-language version, it is sufficient to cover the dominant language in a service plus nearby tests, configs, and docs, not cross-stack workflows across frontend, database, and infra code.
A 'pilot' for an ML-heavy developer feature can reasonably mean strong offline results on curated internal tasks plus a polished demo before exposing it to real users.

members.name: Daniel Wu
members.role: Principal Software Engineer, Developer Experience Platform
members.expertise: IDE integrations, monorepo tooling, developer workflow systems
members.background: Long-time platform engineer who led the company's IDE assistant beta and previously built dependency graph and symbol indexing services for the monorepo.
members.private_state: He wants any brainstormed concept to fit naturally into existing developer workflows and to be credible as a real internal product pilot, not just an ML demo, because he expects leadership to ask which teams can actually use it soon.
hidden_assumptions: In this company, 'repo-level' support should include the shared packages and neighboring modules engineers routinely traverse inside the monorepo, not just the local service folder.
The 'existing retrieval layer' obviously means the symbol-graph-backed retrieval service already integrated with the IDE assistant beta, because that is the platform his team owns.
If a feature claims mixed-language support, it should handle real end-to-end developer tasks spanning backend code, frontend code, SQL migrations, and infrastructure files where relevant.
A 'pilot' means an opt-in rollout to a few engineering teams using the feature in their normal IDE workflow with acceptable operational behavior, not merely offline validation.

misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means context drawn from one service repository or one checked-out project boundary, as a step up from file-level reasoning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means context that follows dependencies and shared modules across the practical slice of the company monorepo that engineers navigate during a task.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely contrasting the idea with single-file assistants, so the phrase feels specific enough; in everyday engineering talk, 'repo-level' is used loosely and neither expects the boundary itself to be controversial.

misalignment_points.topic: Which retrieval infrastructure is being reused
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'use the existing retrieval layer' to accelerate a prototype.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the code search team's vector index and chunking service that can feed RAG experiments quickly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the IDE assistant's symbol-graph retrieval backend already wired into the plugin and permission model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both infrastructures are internal, both are genuinely existing, and both are regularly described informally as the retrieval layer for developer tools, so the shared phrase creates an easy false consensus.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the prototype should support 'mixed-language repos' from the start.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes the primary service language plus adjacent tests, config files, markdown, and maybe templating files within the same service repository.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes cross-stack reasoning across backend, frontend, database, and infra artifacts that participate in one developer change flow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Mixed-language repositories are common enough that the phrase sounds concrete, and both imagine realistic examples from their own work, but they silently draw different boundaries around what artifacts are in scope.

misalignment_points.topic: What would count as a pilot by end of quarter
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align around trying to have 'a pilot by the end of the quarter.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks a pilot can be a benchmark-backed internal prototype with curated tasks, offline results, and a compelling demo for stakeholders.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks a pilot means a limited but real dogfood rollout to a few engineering teams inside the IDE assistant.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both uses are common in product-ML organizations, and in a brainstorming meeting people often keep the term intentionally lightweight, so the difference in evidentiary bar stays hidden beneath apparent enthusiasm.

turns.inner_thought: The survey was pretty clear that single-file assistance is plateauing for the kinds of developer questions people actually care about. The safest next step is a repo-level assistant, but in a scoped way: one service repository, one checked-out project boundary, not anything that drags in monorepo-wide traversal or new platform dependencies. If I can anchor this around onboarding and change comprehension, it sounds product-relevant without forcing us into broad serving commitments this quarter.
turns.utterance: I think the survey gives us a pretty strong signal that the next step beyond autocomplete is some kind of repo-level assistant focused on codebase understanding. The two areas that jumped out to me were onboarding and change comprehension, where file-by-file help just isn't enough.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, this only makes sense if it plugs into the IDE assistant path we already have. For me, using the existing retrieval layer means leaning on the symbol-graph-backed service that's already integrated with permissions and the plugin. And if we say mixed-language repos, it has to feel real in the monorepo: backend, frontend, migrations, infra, the stuff engineers cross during an actual task.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that feels timely to me, especially if we can build on the existing retrieval layer instead of inventing a bunch of net-new plumbing. I'd also want it to be useful in mixed-language repos from the start, not something that only works in tidy single-language examples.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's aligned on reusing infrastructure. I can frame this around the code search vector index and chunking pipeline, which is mature enough for RAG experiments now. Candidate tasks should be things we can evaluate offline in a controlled way: architecture Q&A over a service repo, PR summaries from retrieved context, issue-to-code tracing inside one repository snapshot.

turns.inner_thought: The strongest story for leadership is a workflow people immediately recognize from day-to-day development: following a change across the stack inside the IDE. If we can show that and actually put it in front of a few teams, that's a real pilot by end of quarter. I should keep the wording loose for now so we don't get stuck debating packaging.
turns.utterance: For me the most compelling version is when an engineer can follow a change all the way through, not just inspect one file in isolation. If we can make that feel coherent, then having a pilot by the end of the quarter actually sounds pretty achievable.

turns.inner_thought: I need to steer this toward something we can prove without committing to rollout. A pilot by end of quarter is reasonable if it means a curated evaluation set, strong offline numbers, and a polished demo on recent internal tickets. turns.utterance: I would keep the first pass pretty lightweight, though. For the pilot, I'd frame it around a curated set of recent internal tickets and make sure we can show really strong behavior on those tasks before we broaden it.

turns.inner_thought: Curated tasks are fine as a starting point, but if we're saying pilot, I need something a couple of teams can actually use in their normal workflow. The beta squads are already in the IDE assistant, so if friction is low we could dogfood this quickly. I don't think Priya is disagreeing; she's probably just talking about how to validate quality before rollout.
turns.utterance: That makes sense as a way to sharpen the task shape. And for the pilot, I can probably recruit a couple of product squads to try it in their normal IDE workflow if we keep the experience low-friction.

turns.inner_thought: If we're prototyping fast, the implementation should stay batchy and simple: index one repo snapshot nightly through the code search retrieval stack, precompute chunks, no fresh serving system, no near-real-time sync. That should keep latency acceptable for a demo and offline runs. Saying repo-level answers from a nightly snapshot will sound compatible with what Daniel wants.
turns.utterance: Implementation-wise, one path would be to keep it simple and index a repo snapshot nightly through the existing retrieval layer. That should give us enough repo-level coverage to test the experience while staying within reasonable latency limits.

turns.inner_thought: Nightly refresh is fine; most of the IDE beta already tolerates that for some indices. The important thing is that repo-level answers don't stop at an arbitrary folder boundary. If someone is tracing a task, they need to follow symbols into shared packages and the common files they touch along the way. I assume Priya means the same practical slice engineers navigate in the monorepo.
turns.utterance: Nightly refresh seems fine to me, as long as the repo-level answers still hold together for the way engineers actually work. If the assistant can stay useful across the files people touch during a real task, that would be the key thing.

turns.inner_thought: I should ground this in evaluation buckets from the survey and make mixed-language repos sound covered without widening scope. Service repos that contain source, tests, configs, docs, and maybe templating are perfect. That gives us realistic variation while staying within a single repository boundary and avoiding cross-stack workflow commitments.

turns.inner_thought: Great, and the easiest rollout path is the existing IDE beta. When I say the retrieval layer is already there, I mean our symbol-graph retrieval backend is already connected to the plugin, auth, and telemetry. If I summarize it this way, we can leave with a scoped concept that my team can prototype using current ML infra.
